lines: Biscuit just inspected my shoes. I passed. Narrowly.
That terrier has more appointments than I do. Admirable.
Biscuit and I have an understanding. He leads, I admire.
Biscuit sat down mid-promenade. A fine idea. I joined him.
The terrier sniffed my pocket. Yes, there was a crust. Guilty.
Biscuit has found a leaf. He is very proud. So am I.
I bowed to Biscuit. Biscuit did not bow back. Fair.
A gull is walking beside me. Same pace. Same ambitions.
That gull looked at my hands. No baguette. Not until tomorrow.
The gulls are holding a meeting on the roof. Very long agenda.
One gull, one leg, one chimney. A small masterpiece.
I tried to whistle like a gull. A gull replied. Politely.
The gulls have the best seats in town. Zinc, front row.
A gull just landed on the fountain. Very theatrical entrance.
The cat on the wall has not moved since lunch. My hero.
That cat and I share a philosophy. Warm stone, no plans.
The wall cat blinked at me. I am counting it as a friendship.
I asked the cat for tips on lounging. It yawned. Lesson one.
The cat has moved two centimetres toward the sun. Bold.
Somebody is playing the accordion up the lane. Ah, waltz time.
I am walking in three-four time. It is the accordion's fault.
Humming the same tune since noon. I think I composed it.
There is a radio in a window playing Trenet. Lovely choice.
I know two chords on the guitar. Both are for Camille.
Somewhere a piano is practising scales. Up, down. Very tidy.
Léo wants a drum. Camille wants quiet. I want both, gently.
A whistle, a hum, a little skip. That is my afternoon song.
The string lights are not on yet. They are saving themselves.
My book is in my pocket. I have read page forty eleven times.
Chapter three. The detective has stopped for a long lunch. Ha.
I carry a novel everywhere. It enjoys the walks.
Reading on a stroll is advanced strolling. Please do not try.
The book says the hero walked to the sea. I am doing research.
Bookmark: a café receipt. Very fitting for this chapter.
Henri lent me a book about lemons. I am on chapter citrus.
Crossword, seven across: afternoon nap. Six letters. Sieste.
I solved one crossword clue today. I am resting on it now.
Henri does the crossword in ink. I do it in hope.
Five letters, a pleasant walk. Théo? Four. So close.
I have a crossword pencil. It has never seen an eraser.
Afternoon hobby number one: noticing things. I am very good.
Hobby number two: pointing at clouds. That one is a croissant.
I collect good benches. This town has an excellent collection.
I am learning to juggle. Two oranges. The third is aspirational.
Today's sketch: one cypress. It came out like a small flame.
I keep a little notebook of perfect corners. Page full again.
Photography hobby: I took a picture of a door. A blue door.
Birdwatching report: gulls, gulls, one sparrow, more gulls.
Kite season. Léo flies it, I hold the string's emotional side.
The trick to a stroll is never arriving. I am a professional.
Left at the fountain, right at the cypress, wherever after.
Afternoon routine: walk, pause, admire, repeat. Flawless.
I timed my lap today. Very slow. A personal best.
My office this afternoon: the whole promenade. Nice desk.
This is my working walk. The work is mostly looking at roofs.
I have checked every shutter on the lane. All very blue.
Pause number seven. This one is for the view.
Stroll inspection complete. The town passes with honours.
I tip my hat to every lamp post. They expect it now.
A good afternoon has no edges. You just float through it.
Tomorrow's baguette is already in my thoughts. Planning ahead.
Bread thought of the hour: the crust is the hug of the loaf.
I can smell the bakery from here. Afternoon batch. Fougasse.
A connoisseur never walks past a bakery. He walks past twice.
I am rating the light today. Honey. Nine out of ten.
The palm trees are swaying in time. Someone tuned them.
The cypresses stand so straight. I am trying it. Very tall.
The fountain has been saying the same thing all day. Charming.
The shadows are getting longer. So is my walk. Coincidence.
A bee is visiting every geranium. Thorough. I respect it.
Someone has hung out their laundry. Striped. Very Riviera.
The zinc roofs are shining like freshly polished spoons.
A balcony full of basil. I took a polite sniff. Bravo.
Look at that bougainvillea. Showing off, and rightly so.
The kiosk has new postcards. I will send one to myself.
Marcel just waved a tea towel at me. I waved my book back.
Henri is watering the same pot again. It looks delighted.
Odile told me my collar is crooked. Now it is perfect.
Léo has explained the fountain to me. I understand nothing.
Camille says I wander. I say I curate the afternoon.
Léo wants to know if the cat is retired. I said semi.
A visitor asked me the way. I gave them my favourite one.
A small boy saluted me. I saluted back. Official business.
The best part of the afternoon is that evening comes next.
Nearly rosé o'clock. I can feel it in my shoes.
Five o'clock and all is well. I checked personally.
Almost time to meet Camille at the railing. I rehearse wow.
I have saved my best mood for the golden hour. Nearly there.
My plan for the next hour: more of this exact thing.
Nothing happened this afternoon. It was magnificent.
A man of leisure walks with his hands behind his back. Like so.
I sat on a wall next to the cat. We said nothing. Wonderful.
Biscuit, a gull and the cat in one glance. A full house.
If you see a man smiling at a cypress, that is me. Hello.
I held the café door for Henri. He bowed. I bowed. Lovely.
A breeze off the sea. I have decided it is for me.
Marcel, your awning is magnificent today. Truly.
I told the fountain it looks well. It sparkled harder.
Odile complimented my shirt. I will wear it until Tuesday.
Merci, breeze. That was exactly the right amount.
The lemon trees smell like a good mood.
Henri, the lemons look heroic. Tell them I said so.
I found a coin and gave it to the fountain. Fair is fair.
Warm enough for linen. Not warm enough to stop strolling.
Someone dropped a glove. I put it on the railing, waving.
Thank you, sun, for doing the promenade so evenly.
I am walking slowly so the afternoon lasts longer.
The cypresses are swaying. I sway back. Politely.
The kiosk lady gave me an extra sugar. A queen.
Léo says I walk like a pigeon. A distinguished pigeon.
Camille sent me out for nothing at all. I am excellent at it.
Late summer. The best kind. Do not tell the other seasons.
I said bonjour to every bench. They all said nothing, kindly.
Henri waved his hat at me. I waved my whole arm.
Marcel's geraniums are out in force. Very red. Very proud.
My afternoon has one task: admire. Going very well.
I helped a gull find a crumb. It nodded, I think.
The shade of the plane tree. Five stars. I would return.
Lucie, your basket is beautiful. Obviously, she says.
I picked up Odile's dropped pen. She called me a dear.
The tiles are warm through my shoes. Like a hug for feet.
Today I bought nothing, did nothing, and thanked everyone.
Pausing here. The view asked me to. I could not refuse.
One lap of the fountain, for my health and my joy.
A soft wind, a long shadow, a free afternoon. Merci.
I let a lady go first at the kiosk. She let me go first. We wait.
Afternoon light makes everyone look like a painting.
Henri, you look very well watered yourself today.
That breeze smelled of lavender. Who do I thank?
My compliments to whoever whitewashed that wall. Dazzling.
Léo's friend asked where Léo is. I pointed everywhere.
I walk past the café and nod. Marcel nods. Tradition.
Warm sun, cool shade. I am alternating, scientifically.
Strolling the promenade in one direction. Then the other.
Someone's hat blew off. I caught it. A modest hero.
The palms are clapping. For the weather, I assume.
I told the neighbour his newspaper looks very interesting.
Afternoon walk number one of one. A complete success.
This light is so golden-ish. It is practising for later.
A lovely old man smiled at me. I smiled with interest.
I am carrying nothing. My hands have the afternoon off.
Camille's favourite bench is empty. I am keeping it warm.
The sea is very blue. I approve. I approve every day.
Henri taught me a lemon tip. Water at the roots. Genius.
Lucie zoomed past and said hello twice. Generous.
Even the shadows look relaxed this afternoon.
I complimented a dog. The dog complimented me back. Wag.
Strolling past the arcade. The marquee winks. I wink.
The afternoon is long and soft, like good bread inside.
Swallows overhead. Very busy. I salute their effort.
Odile says my hair looks windswept. That is the plan.
Some afternoons are for doing. This one is for being.
A kid gave me a pebble. I will treasure it. It is round.
The breeze moved my hair to the left. I will allow it.
Smell that? Warm stone and someone's apricot tart.
I am walking at the speed of the clouds. Elegant pace.
Henri held a branch so I could pass. We are gentlemen.
If you need me, I am out here. Being warm.
The fountain is extra splashy. Someone is happy today.
I told the café terrace it looks inviting. Then I sat.
The cypresses keep pointing up. Yes, I see it. Blue sky.
Léo waved at me from the fountain. I waved for a minute.
Strolling with a full heart and an empty schedule.
The breeze brings a little salt. Seasoning for the day.
I offered Odile my arm on the step. She accepted, beaming.
Thank you, afternoon. You have been very kind to me.
My route: the café, the fountain, the café. A classic.
I am thinking about dinner. Lovingly, not urgently.
It is warm, it is quiet, it is mine. And yours.
The neighbour lent me his shade. A true friend.
Camille will ask what I did. I will say: the promenade.
The flower boxes are overflowing. Generous little boxes.
Léo ran round the fountain eleven times. I watched all eleven.
The fountain is doing its one trick. It does it very well.
A child shrieked with joy just now. Excellent shriek. Top marks.
Léo says the fountain is an ocean. I have agreed to be a fish.
I have been appointed referee. The game has no rules. I am thriving.
Léo found a coin in the fountain and put it back. A true gentleman.
Hopscotch chalk on the promenade. I did one square. Very carefully.
The children are racing the pigeons. The pigeons are winning.
Léo asked why water is wet. I said tradition. He accepted it.
A leaf is floating in the fountain. Léo has named it Monsieur Leaf.
I lost at tag on purpose. Léo knows. We both pretend he does not.
Splash on my trousers. The fountain says hello. Hello, fountain.
Léo and his friend are building a kingdom from three pebbles.
My official job this afternoon: holding a stick for Léo. Honoured.
There is a cartwheel competition. I am a judge. Everyone gets gold.
The fountain sparkles at four o'clock. I checked. It is reliable.
Léo wants to be a baker. I have never been so proud of anyone.
Children at the fountain, gulls on the roof. Perfect arrangement.
I taught Léo to skip a stone. Into the fountain. It counted.
Léo has invented a dance called The Théo. It is mostly shrugging.
A small girl just waved at me. I waved back with great ceremony.
The fountain makes rainbows if you stand just here. Come, stand.
Léo is whispering secrets to the fountain. It keeps every one.
Ice cream on Léo's nose. I will tell him in about ten minutes.
Hide and seek. I am hiding behind a palm. A very thin palm.
The windows are starting to blush. The afternoon is getting on.
Soon the string lights. I love the moment just before they come on.
The sun is in every window on the hill. Like they are all home.
Henri's window boxes glow at this hour. Geraniums, fully lit.
Somebody has a lamp on already. Early. Cosy. I approve.
Zinc roofs going golden, one by one. I could watch it all week.
Our kitchen window catches the sun at five. Camille's favourite.
The lamps on the promenade are waiting. Patiently. Like me.
The café has lit its little candles. A touch eager. Lovely.
The shutters are half open everywhere. The town is having a doze.
The kiosk awning throws a stripe of shade. I am standing in it.
Long shadows already. My shadow is very tall. Finally.
Third window from the left, the cat is out. Good afternoon, cat.
One day I will count the windows of this town. Not today.
The bakery window has one croissant left. I am leaving it. Growth.
The light hits the fountain spray just so. Tiny fireworks.
White walls, pink light, blue sky. Somebody planned this.
I am content. I checked twice, to be sure. Yes. Content.
I sat, I stood, I sat again. A full programme.
This is the hour I like best. I say that about every hour.
A breeze through the palms. I closed my eyes. Strongly recommend.
My shoes have done a lovely loop. They deserve a rest. Soon.
Lucky man. Good bread, good wife, good boy, good fountain.
I said bonjour to six people. Six excellent bonjours back.
The quiet here is the good kind. Like a cat on a warm step.
Today I will be grateful for: shade. And the lemon trees. And shade.
Some days you just walk slowly and nod. Today is that day.
I found a bench with my name on it. Not literally. Spiritually.
Is this a nap or a stroll? Both. Strolling with my eyes half shut.
I passed Camille twice. She smiled twice. I am on a winning streak.
Odile has told me three lovely things. I am storing them up.
Afternoon report: sun present, bread eaten, family well.
I could live in this exact afternoon. I mostly already do.
I bought nothing at the kiosk and had a wonderful chat.
Léo gave me a shell. I will keep it forever. Or until dinner.
Every step on the promenade is a little holiday.
Léo says I am the second best dad. He would not say who is first.
The fountain, the gulls and me. A small, happy committee.
Five o'clock. The town exhales. I exhale with it.
The children have gone quiet. Snack time. Wise children.
I offered Léo half my pain au chocolat. He took the bigger half.
Strolling past our house, I waved at it. It is a good house.
Léo has named the fountain Gérard. Gérard seems pleased.
A grandmother and a toddler, feeding crumbs to sparrows. Bravo.
The promenade smells of warm stone and jasmine. I breathe deeply.
My thinking face. I am thinking about nothing. Deeply.
I asked the fountain for a wish. It gave me a nice afternoon.
The bakery is closed for siesta. Respect. I salute the door.
Léo's friend asked if I am famous. Locally, for bread.
A chalk sun drawn by the fountain. Bigger than the real one. Bravo.
Children on the fountain rim, arms out. Tightrope artists, all.
I let Léo choose the route home. We are going the long way. Twice.
The church bell rang five. Then a pigeon added a sixth.
Window boxes, washing lines, a sleepy cat. Peak afternoon.
I am wearing linen. It is the fabric of doing nothing well.
The shade moved, so I moved. We are dancing slowly, the shade and I.
Camille texted a heart. I texted a baguette. She understands.
A wet handprint on the fountain. Léo's size. A little signature.
I have perfected the slow wave. Wrist only. Very elegant.
If someone asks, I was busy all afternoon. Busy being happy.
Practising my waltz for tonight. One, two, three. Mostly three.
I am learning the box step. The box is going very well.
Tonight I will dip Camille. I am practising on the air.
I am rehearsing my toast for tonight. It has nine words now.
Toast draft two: to the sun, to the bread, to Camille. Done.
Henri is teaching me chess. I know how the horse moves. Hop.
I lost to Henri in four moves. He says it was a lovely four.
Odile is teaching me to knit. I have made one long sock-scarf.
Knit one, purl one. Odile says I purl with great confidence.
My scarf is two rows long. By winter it will be a bookmark.
I am learning the names of flowers. That one is Bernadette.
Henri says it is oleander. I still prefer Bernadette.
New word today: plumbago. The blue one. Say it. Plumbago.
I am learning birdsong. That was a sparrow. Or a gate.
Cloud study: cumulus, cumulus, and one that looks like Léo.
Learning to tell the time by shadows. It is about tea-ish.
My shadow says four o'clock. My watch says four. Agreement.
I am practising the two-finger whistle. So far, one finger works.
Whistle attempt eleven. A pigeon turned round. Progress.
Léo is teaching me the yo-yo. It goes down beautifully.
Yo-yo report: down, yes. Up, we are working on it together.
I am learning a card trick from Odile. Pick a card. Any card.
The card trick worked! Odile chose her card for me. Kind.
Practising my bedtime story voices. The wolf is very polite.
Tonight's story needs a dragon voice. I am testing it. Rrr.
I have learned to tie Léo's laces with bunny ears. Two bunnies.
Léo is learning to read. Today he read BOULANGERIE. My boy.
Léo spelled his name in chalk. Then mine. Then 'pain'.
I am learning brioche at home. Flour everywhere. Joy everywhere.
My first brioche looked like a hat. Camille wore it. Then ate it.
Baking lesson: patience. The dough rises when it likes.
I watched the baker fold dough. Like folding a soft letter.
Practising my bonjour. Warm, short, eyes crinkled. Bonjour!
I am learning to sit still. Seven minutes today. A record.
Pétanque lesson from Henri. Gentle throw. The ball rolled home.
I got a boule within a hand of the jack. Henri applauded.
I am learning the harmonica. It knows one song. So do I.
Harmonica practice at the railing. The gulls hum along.
Learning to make paper hats. Léo has a new one every hour.
Paper hat number six. This one has a feather. A gull feather.
Lucie is teaching me bicycle bell etiquette. Two dings, a smile.
Camille is teaching me to fold fitted sheets. A lifelong study.
Today I learned the fountain has four lions. I counted twice.
The baker taught me to tap a loaf. Hollow means good. Tok tok.
Learning to draw Léo. So far, a circle with joy in it.
I am memorising a poem for Camille. Line one is her name.
Léo showed me how to hop on one foot. I can do it. Briefly.
I am learning patience from the lemon trees. They take ages.
I met Camille right here. She dropped a peach. I caught it.
This bench is where I first held Léo. He yawned at the sea.
Léo took his first steps on this promenade. Toward a gull.
Léo's first word was 'pain'. Bread runs in the family.
Our wedding dance was under these lights. I stepped on no one.
I proposed by the fountain. Camille said yes before I asked.
The day we moved in, Henri brought lemons. He still does.
I taught Léo to ride his bike right here. He wobbled, then flew.
Once it snowed here. One morning. The whole town made one snowman.
The summer the café played music every night. We danced every one.
First time Léo saw the string lights, he said 'oh' for a minute.
Odile was at our wedding. She danced longer than any of us.
Camille and I shared our first croissant at that table. Half each.
I remember Léo asleep on my shoulder by the fountain. Heavy, warm.
Our first night here we ate bread on the steps. Best dinner.
Léo's first ice cream. Most of it on his chin. All of it joy.
Henri taught me to prune a lemon tree, years ago. Snip, smile.
The day Léo was born, Marcel gave everyone a free coffee.
I still have the cork from our first rosé here. In a drawer.
Last summer we picnicked under that palm. Léo named the ants.
Camille laughed so hard here once she had to sit on the fountain.
This is where Léo lost his first tooth. In a baguette. Fitting.
Every spring we measure Léo against the kiosk. He gains a postcard.
I learned to say 'takk' from a neighbour. Takk, sun. Takk, shade.
I asked for baguette in Norwegian. Baguett. Close enough. Takk.
I am learning to walk slower. I was already very good.
Lesson from Léo: every puddle deserves a jump. Even a small one.
Learning to balance a spoon on my nose. For Léo. For science.
I know three constellations now. Tonight I will show Léo one.
I am learning the café menu by heart. Citron pressé is my anthem.
Marcel taught me to carry three cups. I carried two. Bravo, me.
I took a watercolour class. The sky came out exactly this blue.
Learning to name every house on the lane. Ours is the happiest.
Practising my compliments. Odile, that cardigan sings.
I am learning to knead with both hands. One hand keeps waving.
Camille taught me to make lemonade. Henri's lemons, our sugar.
Lesson nine of strolling: let the breeze choose at corners.
Our first Christmas here, the whole lane sang under one lamp.
I used to get lost in this town. Now I get lost on purpose.
The first time I bought bread here, the baker added a smile. Free.
I am practising my French accent. I am French. It is going well.
Léo is teaching me hopscotch rules. There are forty. He invents them.
Learning to fold a napkin into a swan. Mine is a confident duck.
Camille and I danced on this exact tile at our first fête.
The bougainvillea has gone purple in the dusk. Showing off.
To the lemon tree on our balcony. Three lemons and counting.
Tomorrow I water the geraniums. Today I admire them.
The hollyhocks by the door are taller than me now. Unfair.
Plan for tomorrow: one baguette, one lemon tart, one long nap.
I have named our lemon tree Gérard. He is thriving.
Léo planted a sunflower seed today. He checked it six times.
My father grew tomatoes like little suns. I grow opinions.
A glass, a wife, a bougainvillea. A man needs nothing else.
Henri gave me a cutting of his lemon tree. I feel knighted.
Tomorrow, croissants. I am telling the glass so it holds me to it.
The lavender pots are asleep. I will tiptoe past them.
Santé to the jasmine. It works the night shift.
My grandmother said a garden is just patience in a pot.
The ice clinks. The cicadas agree. Perfect evening.
I pruned the rosemary today. Then I ate some. Efficient.
Camille says I talk to the lemon tree. I say it listens.
Look at the cypresses, all standing up straight for the lamps.
This is my professional sitting. I trained for years.
Next week I build Léo a little window box. Probably next week.
Our first date was on this terrace. I ordered the wrong wine.
I chose a cold one tonight. My finest work this week.
The basil on our sill smells like every summer at once.
A little toast to the bougainvillea. It climbed all day.
When I was Léo's age, I hid in my uncle's fig tree. Still do.
The lemon blossom is out. Smell that. That is the whole town.
Camille's cheeks match the rosé. I will not mention it. Oh.
Our door is half bougainvillea now. We just walk through flowers.
One glass, maybe two. Gérard the lemon tree will not tell.
Léo wants to plant a baguette to grow a baguette tree. I support this.
The terrace is cool, the stone is warm. Everything is right.
I watered the geraniums at noon. They are still grateful.
To the sky. It put on its best blue for us.
My mother pressed flowers in her cookbooks. Every recipe bloomed.
I have decided to enjoy this slowly. Very slowly. Watch me.
The oleander is pink, the door is blue. Someone planned this.
Even the cactus by the café wears a little flower tonight.
Rosé with Camille at blue hour. I have peaked. Happily.
The palm by the fountain has a new leaf. I saw it first.
Léo is asleep with a pine cone in his hand. A collector.
A lemon tree, a terrace, a table for two. My entire plan.
This glass is the colour of the oleander. I matched it.
The window boxes are lit by the lamps. Tiny flower theatres.
I am pacing myself. One sip per lamp.
Cold glass, warm evening, nowhere to be. Officially busy.
I promised Léo a strawberry patch. I have bought one strawberry.
The cicadas are tuning up. Front row seats, Camille.
Gérard, you look magnificent tonight. There. Ripen.
To the bakery, which opens again in eleven hours. Not long.
We painted our door blue the summer Léo was born.
I will finish this glass and then I will finish this view.
The roses by the kiosk are blushing. Like the sky. Like me.
Tomorrow Léo and I repot the basil. He calls it gardening day.
Camille laughed at my toast. Best review I have ever had.
The fig tree on the corner is heavy again. Saturday, figs.
Santé to everyone with a lemon tree. Santé to Henri twice.
My aunt grew bougainvillea so thick the postman got lost in it.
I have a plan. Sit here. Then keep sitting here.
The petunias have closed for the night. Very sensible petunias.
Our lemon tree came in a pot the size of a teacup. Look now.
I propose a toast to the hollyhocks. Long may they lean.
Léo whispered goodnight to the tomato plant. It heard.
Camille, smell the air. Salt and jasmine. Bottle it.
The lamps came on and the glass got rosier. Science.
My father taught me to tie up tomatoes. I tie up everything now.
Pink drink, blue hour, gold lamps. I am living in a painting.
There is a geranium on every sill on this street. I counted.
To the evening, which arrived exactly when I sat down. Manners.
The lemon tree needs a bigger pot. Saturday's grand project.
Every bougainvillea in town seems to be leaning toward the café.
This is a working evening. I am working on contentment.
Camille's mother sent us lavender seeds. Next spring, purple.
One more clink before the stars. Tradition since Tuesday.
The palms are rustling. They have gossip. Good gossip.
Our olive tree has three olives. A modest, dignified tree.
Tomorrow I ask Henri the secret of his lemons. Again.
The terrace smells of thyme. Someone stepped on it lovingly.
Léo wants a pumpkin by October. We have planted hope.
A quiet glass after a busy day of strolling. I earned it.
Look, the moonflowers are opening. Late risers, like me.
Camille, I believe this is our best blue hour. As always.
The glass is empty, the evening is full. Fair trade.
Rosé at blue hour. The colours are having a meeting.
Pink glass, blue sky. I am colour-coordinated by accident.
A small sip. A medium sip. I am pacing myself, nobly.
This glass is half full. I checked twice. Still half full.
I propose a toast to the shutters. Closed for the night. Well done.
Santé to the fountain. It never takes an evening off.
One glass of rosé. Two olives. A perfect ratio.
I raise my glass to the gulls. They do not raise theirs.
This is my thinking face. I am thinking about olives.
Léo is asleep. The rosé and I may now speak freely.
Rosé, from the French for: yes, one more minute.
I am not drinking. I am tasting the evening.
Camille says I hold my glass like a violin. Thank you.
Clink. That was the official start of the evening.
This rosé tastes of apricots and of not doing the dishes.
To the string lights. You hang about beautifully.
I tried to describe this sky. I ran out of blues.
Henri lifted his hat to my glass. I lifted my glass to his hat.
Pastis was considered. Pastis was politely declined.
Another toast? To toasts. They are so easy to make.
Marcel's pour: generous, theatrical, slightly to the left.
A moth is inspecting my glass. Sorry, friend, it is booked.
We have one bowl of crisps and no plans at all. Paradise.
Camille and I clink, then the fountain splashes. Applause.
I am on my second glass. Of water. Then the rosé. Strategy.
Sip, sigh, look at the sea. Repeat as needed.
A rosé this cold deserves a sky this calm.
I hold the glass up and the whole town fits inside it. Pink.
Yusuf asked what I am celebrating. Tuesday, Yusuf. Tuesday.
The olive stone goes in the little dish. Civilisation.
To the baguette from this morning. Gone, never forgotten.
Camille, the wine has legs. Do not worry, it is not leaving.
The clock tower says twenty past eight. It is always right.
The tiles on the fountain look bluer now. Their favourite hour.
Biscuit has found the exact centre of the warm paving.
That cat has not moved in an hour. I respect the commitment.
A gull just walked past like it owns the promenade. It does.
The kiosk light is on. It looks like a little lantern.
The fountain is talking to itself again. Splish, splash.
Biscuit sneezed at a lavender bush. Bless you, monsieur.
The zinc roofs go blue first. Then the walls. Then me.
Blue hour: when the town puts on its slippers.
Is it night yet? Not yet. It is in the hallway.
